stories.headline: Nasdaq jumps 1.1% as AI chip stocks bounce back after a rough week
stories.dek: Intel, AMD and Micron led the rebound. The Dow slipped a little. Oil stayed above $100.
stories.caveman: Last week was bad for tech stocks. On Monday they came back. The Nasdaq (a list full of tech companies) rose 1.11% to 26,430.89. The S&P 500 rose 0.41% to 7,690.73. The Dow fell just 36 points to 51,966.03. Chip makers did best: Intel rose about 2% after JPMorgan bank said it likes the stock more now, AMD rose 1.8% and memory maker Micron rose about 3%. One AI cloud company, CoreWeave, still fell a bit after losing about a quarter of its value last week, and the price of insurance against it failing to pay its debt is at worrying levels. Oil is still very expensive: US oil (WTI) rose 2.2% to $103.66 a barrel. This week Meta and Tesla report how much money they made.
stories.why_it_matters: Many people's retirement money sits in these stock lists. Investors keep swinging between "AI will make huge profits" and "AI spending is a bubble." Oil above $100 also keeps gas and shipping prices high.
stories.camps: Bulls: AI demand is real; Anthropic told investors its quarterly sales hit $16.8 billion, and chip makers are selling everything they make. Bears: research firm Gartner says about $3.5 trillion in AI investment could be at risk because profits are not yet keeping up, and bond investors are shunning debt-heavy AI cloud companies like CoreWeave.
stories.image_alt: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange
stories.image_credit: Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A US stock list packed with tech companies like Apple, Nvidia and Microsoft.
A list of 500 big US companies. People use it as a score for the whole US stock market.
When a bank's analysts say a stock is now a better buy than before.
A kind of insurance investors buy in case a company can't pay back its debt. When it gets pricey, people are worried.
West Texas Intermediate, the main price for US crude oil.

stories.headline: China's economy grows 4.5% as AI-related exports boom, but home building keeps sinking
stories.dek: Factories are humming and exports jumped. Shoppers are still holding back, and property investment fell more than 20%.
stories.caveman: China said its economy grew 4.5% from July to September compared with a year earlier. That beat what experts guessed and was faster than the 4.3% in spring. For the first nine months, growth is 4.6%, inside the government's goal of 4.5% to 5%. Factories made 5.5% more stuff in September, but shop sales grew only 1.1%. The big engine is selling things abroad: exports jumped by more than a third in September, helped by AI electronics and cars. But the inside of the economy is weak. Money spent on new buildings, roads and machines fell 7.2% this year, and money put into property fell 20.6%.
stories.why_it_matters: China is the world's second-biggest economy and Taiwan's biggest trading partner. If China grows by selling more abroad while its own people buy less, other countries may complain about a flood of cheap Chinese goods.
stories.camps: Upbeat view: Beijing hit its targets without new stimulus, and high-tech factories are moving up the value ladder (Pantheon economist Duncan Wrigley). Worried view: growth leans too hard on exports and the AI boom; the housing slump and weak shoppers have not been fixed, and the Iran conflict is still a drag (ABN Amro).
stories.image_alt: Packages move along a conveyor belt at a Chinese logistics centre
stories.image_credit: Photo: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Gross domestic product: the total value of everything a country makes and sells. Its growth rate is a report card for the economy.
Compared with the same period one year earlier.
Money spent on long-lasting things like factories, roads, buildings and machines.
Extra government spending or cheap loans to push the economy to grow faster.
How much people spend in shops and online. It shows if regular people feel confident.

stories.headline: France's riots spook markets: borrowing costs hit their highest since 2002
stories.dek: French stocks, bonds and the euro all fell as unrest piled on top of an already big debt problem.
stories.caveman: France already owes a lot of money and runs a budget gap of about 5% of its economy. Now a week of riots has made investors more nervous. On Monday the interest rate France pays to borrow money for 10 years jumped more than 0.1 percentage point, touching its highest level since 2002. The gap between what France and Germany pay to borrow grew to its widest since the euro debt crisis. The main Paris stock list, the CAC 40, fell 1.7%, and the euro dipped slightly. Mike Bell of RBC BlueBay Asset Management summed up the trap: if France cuts spending, people protest; if it doesn't, bond markets punish it — "either the bond markets riot, or the people riot, or both."
stories.why_it_matters: When a country pays more to borrow, there is less money left for schools, hospitals and pensions. France is the euro area's second-biggest economy, so its trouble can spread to its neighbours.
stories.camps: Worried: investors see a political dead end — no government can cut the deficit without more anger in the streets. Calmer: Ken Egan of ratings agency KBRA pointed to last week's bond sales, which showed buyers still have solid demand for French debt.
stories.image_alt: Thousands of protesters march in Paris on October 17, 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Elise Cabane/AFP/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: The interest rate a government pays when it borrows by selling bonds. Higher yield = investors want more pay for the risk.
When a government spends more than it collects in taxes in a year.
The main list of 40 big companies on the Paris stock market.
The gap between two interest rates, here what France pays versus what Germany pays.
The 2010–2012 period when several euro countries, like Greece, struggled to pay their debts.

stories.headline: Indonesia's stock market plunges 5% to a six-year low over fears of being kicked out of a key index
stories.dek: Index company MSCI proposed moving Indonesia out of its 'emerging markets' group. Goldman says $5.6 billion could leave.
stories.caveman: Big investment funds often buy whatever is on lists made by a company called MSCI. On Friday, MSCI proposed moving Indonesia out of its 'emerging markets' list and into a small 'stand-alone' group. On Monday, Jakarta's main stock index fell more than 5%, to its lowest since October 2020. Goldman Sachs bank guessed that funds that copy the list automatically would have to sell about $5.6 billion of Indonesian stocks. MSCI will decide by June, depending on whether Indonesia makes its market more open and better run. MSCI's Indonesia index has already fallen 47% this year, and foreigners have pulled out about $5.1 billion.
stories.why_it_matters: Indonesia is Southeast Asia's biggest economy. Money leaving its market can weaken its currency and make life pricier for its people. It also shows how much power a few index companies have over whole countries.
stories.camps: Pessimists: Goldman still says avoid Indonesian stocks — weak company profits and rule uncertainty mean the bottom may not be in. Optimists: stocks are now very cheap compared with profits, and if Indonesia fixes transparency before June, the downgrade could be avoided.
stories.image_alt: The Semanggi overpass in Jakarta, Indonesia
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A company that makes stock lists (indexes). Trillions of dollars in funds follow its lists.
A country whose economy is growing and opening up but isn't yet 'rich', like Indonesia or Brazil.
A fund that just copies an index instead of picking stocks. If a country leaves the index, the fund must sell.
Being moved to a lower category, which can scare investors away.
The main stock index of Indonesia's stock exchange.

stories.headline: Musk says he'll give one SpaceX share to every US kid; Anthropic sets aside 5% of its shares for the 'public good'
stories.dek: Two AI-era giants pledged big giveaways as pressure grows over what AI will do to jobs.
stories.caveman: AI company Anthropic (maker of the Claude chatbot) said on Sunday it will put 5% of its shares into a Public Benefit Fund, and more as the company's value grows. The money could go to charities, to groups hit by AI, or to study how AI replaces jobs. Anthropic says none of it will be used for lobbying or political donations. Elon Musk replied that shares should go straight to the public. On Monday he posted that next year he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. CNBC counted about 72 million US kids, so that would be about $10.5 billion at Friday's price. He did not say how it would work.
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies are about to become some of the most valuable on Earth, while many people fear losing their jobs to AI. Who shares in that wealth is becoming a big political question.
stories.camps: Supporters: giving ordinary people and kids a slice of these companies spreads the wealth; Invest America founder Brad Gerstner called Musk's plan possibly the biggest gift ever. Skeptics: there are no details yet; CNBC notes Musk has a spotty record on past giving pledges (like a promised $1 billion to OpenAI that ended at about $38 million), and both companies are preparing for or riding huge stock listings, so the pledges also work as PR.
stories.image_alt: Elon Musk
stories.image_credit: Photo: Reuters via BBC News

terms.explain: A tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company grows, the share is worth more.
Anthropic's new pot of company shares meant to pay for things that help the public.
Initial public offering: when a company first sells shares on the stock market.
Paying people to push politicians to make rules you like.
Giving money away to help others, usually by rich people.

stories.headline: US bans Chinese AI DeepSeek from civilian government agencies
stories.dek: Homeland Security made the order public Monday. It quietly took effect at the end of July and covers tools built with DeepSeek too.
stories.caveman: DeepSeek is a Chinese AI model that is free and cheap to use, so lots of people and companies use it. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has now banned it across civilian government agencies — like the Treasury, the State Department and the Justice Department. The ban also covers any technology built with help from DeepSeek's models. The military's agencies are not included. DHS made the order public on Monday, but it has been in force since the end of July. DHS did not say exactly what the security worry is. American AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have accused some Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, of copying their models.
stories.why_it_matters: This is another step in the US–China AI race. Some US tech companies (like Snowflake and Vercel) offer DeepSeek to their customers, so rules for government could later spread to business.
stories.camps: For the ban: the Trump White House says Chinese firms have exploited American AI, and officials don't want government data flowing into tools tied to a rival country. Against or cautious: DeepSeek is open source and widely used because it's cheap; critics of blanket bans say they can hurt competition and research, and DHS hasn't publicly explained the specific risk. DeepSeek and the Chinese embassy had not commented.
stories.image_alt: The DeepSeek logo shown on a smartphone screen
stories.image_credit: Photo: CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images, via BBC News

terms.explain: A Chinese AI company whose chatbot and models are free and cheap, making it a big rival to US AI firms.
The US government department in charge of border, immigration and domestic security.
Software whose code is shared openly so anyone can use or change it.
Government offices that aren't part of the military, like the Treasury or State Department.
The trained 'brain' behind an AI tool like a chatbot.

stories.headline: Report: 'nudify' apps are easy for 13-year-olds to download despite Apple and Google parental controls
stories.dek: Researchers using test accounts set to age 13 downloaded 135 apps that can strip clothes off people in photos.
stories.caveman: 'Nudify' apps use AI to make fake nude pictures of real people from normal photos. In US high schools, some students have used them on classmates. A watchdog group, the Tech Transparency Project, made four test accounts on Apple and Google phones, all saying the user was 13. Searching terms like "AI video generator," they could download 135 apps with tools to undress people or put faces on nude bodies. (The researchers tested on AI-made women, not real photos.) A Pennsylvania mother, Morgan Dorfman, told the Guardian a student made sexual videos of her daughter and five other girls with one such app.
stories.why_it_matters: Fake nude images can wreck a young person's life and are a form of sexual abuse. Parents rely on phone parental controls, and this report says those controls aren't stopping these apps.
stories.camps: Critics: app stores profit from these apps and their age filters are failing kids; laws banning them aren't being enforced well enough. Apple and Google: both say they ban nudify apps and remove ones they find; Google said it suspended violating apps in this case, and Apple said many apps in the report are normal photo editors that can't make nudes.
stories.image_alt: A person looks at a phone screen in the dark (illustrative photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Spencer Platt/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: An app that uses AI to make fake nude images of a person from an ordinary photo.
A fake but realistic photo, video or voice made with AI.
Phone settings that let parents limit what apps and content kids can get.
A US watchdog group that researches big tech companies.
Done without the person agreeing to it.

stories.headline: Ex-OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a meeting room held without bail; judge calls Saudi bail offer 'problematic'
stories.dek: Prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan hid a recording device in a TV at OpenAI's headquarters. Saudi Arabia offered to pay his bail.
stories.caveman: Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, is a Saudi citizen who worked as an engineer at OpenAI. Prosecutors say on Sept. 28 he hid a recording device inside a TV in an executive meeting room at OpenAI's San Francisco office. On Monday, federal judge Alex Tse ordered him kept in jail until trial, saying he might flee. The Saudi consulate offered to pay his full bail; the judge called it "problematic" and like "a blank check." Saudi Arabia has no deal to send suspects back to the US. Prosecutors also say OpenAI executives met government officials in that room around that time, and more serious charges could come. He faces up to five years if convicted. Next court date: Nov. 6.
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies now hold secrets that governments care about. This case shows spying fears around AI labs are real, and it could test US–Saudi relations.
stories.camps: Prosecution: strong family and money ties to Saudi Arabia make him a flight risk, and the bugging could threaten US national security. Defense side: he has dozens of supporters in court, has not been convicted, and the Saudi government promised supervision and no travel papers; so far he is charged only with trying to intercept conversations.
stories.image_alt: Justice Department photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office
stories.image_credit: Photo: US Department of Justice via CNBC

terms.explain: Money paid so a person accused of a crime can wait for trial outside jail.
A worry that a suspect will run away (often abroad) before trial.
An agreement between countries to send suspects back to face trial.
A country's government office in a foreign city that helps its citizens there.
To secretly catch or record other people's communications.

stories.headline: France orders curfews in parts of Paris and other cities as minister admits police 'lost control'
stories.dek: Over 2,500 people have been arrested. Unions called new strikes for Nov. 5. The PM says a state of emergency is possible.
stories.caveman: France has had weeks of high school student protests, and last weekend some marches turned into riots and looting. On Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered partial curfews: 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities including Lille, and 11pm to 6am in two Paris areas — Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police "lost control": they expected 200,000 protesters but more than 500,000 came. He offered to quit; President Macron said no. About 2,000 shops were looted, almost 1,000 police were hurt, and 2,513 people were arrested, with 67 jailed. Protesters also blocked the Louvre museum. Unions want new strikes on Nov. 5.
stories.why_it_matters: France picks a new president in about six months and is already struggling with debt. Weeks of anger in the streets can shape who wins and what policies come next.
stories.camps: Government: order must be restored; Lecornu says targeted curfews are better than closing whole cities, but a state of emergency is not ruled out. Protesters and unions: most of the 500,000+ marchers were peaceful; they denounce "police repression", say violent groups on the fringes hijacked the day, and are pushing on with strikes rather than backing down.
stories.image_alt: Rioters smash a shop window during the unrest in France
stories.image_credit: Photo: Carl Court/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: A rule that people must stay off the streets during certain hours.
A legal step that gives the government extra powers for a short time in a crisis.
The minister in charge of police and public safety.
Breaking into shops and stealing during unrest.
The famous Paris art museum that holds the Mona Lisa.

stories.headline: Putin reportedly floats a Trump–Xi–Putin summit on Ukraine — without Zelenskyy
stories.dek: The Wall Street Journal says the idea came up in an Oct. 9 call. Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv overnight.
stories.caveman: According to the Wall Street Journal, Russian President Vladimir Putin suggested to Donald Trump in an Oct. 9 phone call that he, Trump and China's Xi Jinping meet to end the Ukraine war — with no Ukrainian leader there. It could happen at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been "talks of a meeting" but he didn't know if it was final. Meanwhile, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and more than 200 drones across Ukraine; President Zelenskyy said 550,000 households lost power. Late Monday, Ukrainian officials said a drone strike near a park café in the Kharkiv region killed at least six people, including a toddler and an 11-year-old girl. Ukraine and the US are also arguing over whether US intelligence sharing was interrupted.
stories.why_it_matters: A deal about Ukraine made without Ukraine would be a huge change. It also gives China a bigger say in Europe's biggest war, which matters for Taiwan too.
stories.camps: Trump side: Trump is open to anything that could end the war, and Rubio denies intelligence sharing was cut. Ukraine and critics: Zelenskyy says easing sanctions on Russia makes the war last longer, and leaving Kyiv out of talks would let big powers decide its fate; some Republicans and European allies are also alarmed.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump greets Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025
stories.image_credit: Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A meeting of top leaders from different countries.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a yearly meeting of Pacific Rim economies.
A fast rocket that flies high and falls on its target, very hard to stop.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another country.
When one country passes spy and warning information to another, like early alerts of missile launches.

stories.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines in critical condition after a car allegedly rammed her twice outside her office
stories.dek: Witnesses say the driver made a U-turn to hit her. A barber pulled the man out of the car. Police arrested a 43-year-old.
stories.caveman: Helen Haines is an independent member of Australia's parliament. On Monday, near her office in Wangaratta, Victoria, a Toyota Land Cruiser allegedly hit her, pinning her against a car — then reversed and hit her again. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said witnesses described the driver making a U-turn to get into the car park. A barber next door, Ricky Jefferies, ran over, pulled the driver out and held him until police came; he said the man had a knife but threw it away. Police arrested a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee. Haines was flown to a Melbourne hospital for emergency surgery and is in critical condition. Burke said there were 1,067 reports of threats or harassment against top office holders last year, up from 951.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on politicians are rising in many democracies. When leaders are not safe meeting voters, it hurts everyone's ability to be heard.
stories.camps: This is not a left-right fight; the government praised the bystander who stopped the driver. The open questions: police have not yet said the motive, so whether it was a targeted political attack is still unconfirmed, and the government is reviewing whether more could have been done to protect MPs.
stories.image_alt: Independent MP Helen Haines
stories.image_credit: Photo: Mick Tsikas/AAP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A member of parliament who doesn't belong to any political party.
An MP's local office where voters can come to meet them.
Very badly hurt; life may be in danger.
Australia's minister in charge of security, police agencies and borders.
The reason someone commits a crime.

stories.headline: Israeli police detain 10 in rare raid on settlers after attacks on US photojournalist and European diplomats
stories.dek: Photographer Heidi Levine had four vertebrae broken. Rights groups say most settler violence against Palestinians goes unpunished.
stories.caveman: In the occupied West Bank, US photojournalist Heidi Levine was covering the olive harvest on Friday when masked Israeli men beat and kicked her; she suffered broken bones in her back. The next day, settlers with sticks and iron bars attacked European diplomats and Palestinians picking olives near Taybeh. On Monday, Israeli police said they detained 10 people tied to the attacks on foreigners and to an illegal outpost; a court kept six of them in custody for three to four more days. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu questioned the accounts, calling them "alleged" and "unproven." The US secretary of state and US ambassador criticized the attacks. Israeli rights group Yesh Din counted 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in three weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: It took attacks on foreigners to trigger arrests. Palestinians face this kind of violence often, and rights groups say 94% of investigations end without charges.
stories.camps: Israeli government and police: Netanyahu cast doubt on the reports; police released raid footage and say they are pursuing those tied to the attacks on foreigners. Critics: Levine, Yesh Din and foreign governments say settlers act with near-total impunity, and the double standard — fast action only when foreigners are hurt — shows the system protects attackers.
stories.image_alt: Photojournalist Heidi Levine in a hospital bed
stories.image_credit: Photo: Debbie Hill/UPI/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: Palestinian land that Israel has occupied since 1967.
Israelis who live in settlements built on occupied Palestinian land.
A small settlement built without Israeli government approval; illegal even under Israeli law.
Getting away with doing wrong without any punishment.
An Israeli human rights group that tracks violence against Palestinians.

stories.headline: HOT: New Larry David biography 'Emperor of Nothing' gets called the definitive portrait of the Seinfeld creator
stories.dek: The Guardian's critic praises Blake J Harris's authorised biography of the comedy legend who kept trying to quit.
stories.caveman: Larry David co-created Seinfeld and stars in Curb Your Enthusiasm. A new authorised biography, Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David by Blake J Harris (HarperCollins), is getting strong reviews; the Guardian calls it "the definitive portrait." David agreed to it by email with: "Oh Jesus. If we must." The book shows a man who kept walking away: he stormed off stages as a young stand-up in 1970s New York, quit his first TV job, and twice quit Seinfeld. Fellow comics once thought he was the least likely to succeed. He was 41 when he started writing the Seinfeld pilot with Jerry Seinfeld. Because David is a fairly decent guy with old friends, Harris could talk to almost everyone important in his life.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a fun read about how one of TV's most famous comedy minds succeeded without much ambition — and a hot pick for gift season.
stories.camps: Fans: the review says it nails why David is funny and how his life turned into his material. Caveat: authorised biographies tend to flatter their subjects, and the critic notes there isn't much dirt — readers wanting scandal won't find it.
stories.image_alt: Larry David in the HBO comedy series Curb Your Enthusiasm
stories.image_credit: Photo: John P. Johnson/HBO via The Guardian

terms.explain: A life story written with the subject's permission and help.
A hugely popular 1990s US sitcom, famous as a 'show about nothing'.
Larry David's HBO comedy show where he plays a cranky version of himself.
Comedy where one person tells jokes alone on stage to an audience.
The first test episode of a TV show, made to convince a network to order more.

stories.headline: HOT: HarperCollins and Netflix launch a wave of Narnia books ahead of Greta Gerwig's film
stories.dek: Tie-in paperbacks, new box sets and a graphic novel are coming before 'Narnia: The Magician's Nephew' hits theaters in February.
stories.caveman: Greta Gerwig (who directed Barbie and Little Women) made a movie of C.S. Lewis's 1955 Narnia book The Magician's Nephew — its first time on screen. It comes to theaters worldwide on Feb. 12, 2027, then to Netflix on April 2. Publisher HarperCollins and Netflix announced a big book push to go with it. In November: a movie-cover paperback (English and Spanish), a new seven-book box set with covers by the film's concept artist Vance Kovacs, hardcover sets, deluxe collector's editions, and store-exclusive versions. A graphic novel by Eisner Award winner Ben Hatke comes Jan. 12, 2027. The seven Narnia books have sold more than 120 million copies in 70 countries.
stories.why_it_matters: Big movies send millions of people back to the books. This shows how publishers now plan whole product lines around streaming films.
stories.camps: Excited: HarperCollins' Liate Stehlik calls the film a coming "cultural event" and says the books will pull new readers into Narnia. Skeptical view: so many editions and store exclusives can feel more like merchandising than reading — fans may end up buying the same story several times.
stories.image_alt: Covers of the Narnia: The Magician's Nephew tie-in edition and new box set
stories.image_credit: Image: Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: A book edition released to go with a movie or show, often with the film's poster on the cover.
All the books in a series sold together in one box.
A book-length story told in comic-book style.
The top US award for comics.
The artist who draws how a film's worlds and characters should look before filming.

stories.headline: TREND: Why do so many buzzy novels never tell you the narrator's name?
stories.dek: A Literary Hub essay looks at the nameless narrators in hit books by Katie Kitamura, Ben Lerner, Deborah Levy and Rachel Cusk.
stories.caveman: In many recent literary novels, the person telling the story ('I') never gets a name. Writer Ilana Bean noticed this when she finished books and tried to Google them — she didn't know what to call the main character. Her Literary Hub essay lists recent talked-about examples: Audition by Katie Kitamura, Transcription by Ben Lerner, My Year in Paris with Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy, and Life of M by Rachel Cusk. She notes a critic called it an "epidemic" back in 2015, and it hasn't slowed. One common idea is that a nameless narrator lets readers step into the character's shoes. Bean isn't sure that works — and asks what these books want readers to notice.
stories.why_it_matters: If you've read a 'quiet, moody city novel' lately, you've likely met this trick. Knowing about it helps you read these books more sharply.
stories.camps: Fans of the style: no name can show a shaky sense of self (like the unnamed second Mrs de Winter in Rebecca) and keeps focus on thoughts, not plot. Doubters: Bean, who enjoys these books, says the trick has become so common it's unclear what it adds, and a name isn't really what stops readers from connecting.
stories.image_alt: Rows of blank 'Hello my name is' name tags
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub

terms.explain: The voice telling the story in a book.
Novels focused on style, character and ideas more than fast plot.
A story told by 'I'.
A common, accepted way of doing something in writing.
Daphne du Maurier's 1938 novel; its narrator, the second Mrs de Winter, is never named.

stories.headline: NOT: 'The Time Traveler's Wife' sequel 'Life Out of Order' disappoints the Guardian's critic
stories.dek: Audrey Niffenegger's 560-page follow-up swaps the love story for a crowded dystopia.
stories.caveman: Audrey Niffenegger's 2003 novel The Time Traveler's Wife was a giant hit: more than 9 million copies in 40 languages, plus a Hollywood film and an HBO show. Now there's a sequel, Life Out of Order. Henry is dead but still pops in from the past, and his daughter Alba has inherited time travel — and is married to different men in past, present and future. Does it match the original's unsettling power? The Guardian's reviewer sums up the 560 pages in one word: no. She says the first book worked because it was a simple love story underneath, but this one chases too many ideas and lands in yet another dystopia.
stories.why_it_matters: Sequels to beloved books sell on nostalgia. This review is a warning to lower expectations before you buy.
stories.camps: Not hot: the critic says it lacks a strong emotional thread and spreads itself thin. On the other hand: it's one review — longtime fans curious about Alba and the world of the original may still want to try it.
stories.image_alt: Author Audrey Niffenegger
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lucy Hewett/The Guardian

terms.explain: A book or film that continues an earlier story.
A story set in a frightening, broken future society.
Moving backward or forward in time, here as a genetic trait.
A critic's opinion piece judging a book.
A time-travel puzzle where an event causes itself, so there's no clear start.

stories.headline: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murders after telling followers to starve their children
stories.dek: All but one of the victims were children. 28 other cult leaders were convicted too. Sentencing is set for Nov. 6.
stories.caveman: Paul Mackenzie led a doomsday cult in Kenya. He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus," and taught that school and modern medicine were evil. In 2023, more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near Kenya's coast. On Monday, a judge in Mombasa found him guilty of murdering 191 people — all but one were children. Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder; they all said no one was forced to die. Sentencing is set for Nov. 6. One father, Stephen Mwiti, lost all six of his children; his ex-wife was among those convicted.
stories.why_it_matters: It is one of the deadliest cult cases in modern history. The children who died were denied food, school and medicine because adults followed one man's teachings.
stories.camps: The prosecution side: the judge said followers saw Mackenzie as "Jesus's mouthpiece", and one co-accused testified he said anyone who resisted fasting should be forced "through kicks and blows". The defence: Mackenzie and his co-accused pleaded not guilty and insisted fasting was voluntary. Mackenzie still faces other cases, including terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.
stories.image_alt: Cult leader Paul Mackenzie (centre)
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images, via BBC News

terms.explain: A group that follows a leader with extreme beliefs and tight control over members.
The forest near Kenya's coast where the cult lived and where the graves were found.
A court's decision on whether someone is guilty.
When the judge decides the punishment after a guilty verdict.
Other people charged in the same case.

stories.headline: Drone strike near a market in Sudan kills 80, many of them people heading home
stories.dek: The attack hit a transport hub in al-Dibab, West Kordofan. The RSF's administration blames the army.
stories.caveman: Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between the army (SAF) and a paramilitary group called the RSF. On Sunday evening, a drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, at a transport hub near the market in al-Dibab, West Kordofan, where people gather to ride home to their villages. A witness said he helped bury 50 bodies, including his brother; a medic said 30 more of the injured died, making 80 dead. It is one of the deadliest single strikes of the war. The RSF controls this area, and its administration, called Tasis, accused the army. Drones caused at least 880 civilian deaths from January to April this year.
stories.why_it_matters: Sudan has one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises, with hundreds of thousands killed and millions forced from home, yet it gets little attention.
stories.camps: RSF side: says the army killed civilians. Army side: in earlier strikes it said it hit RSF fighters, not civilians. The UN: its political chief Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council both sides think they can win by force and foreign backers keep fuelling them — with no breakthrough in sight.
stories.image_alt: A man stands in a hole filled with drone parts in El Obeid, Sudan (March photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Los Angeles Times/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group fighting Sudan's army.
Sudanese Armed Forces, Sudan's national army, led by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.
An armed group organised like an army but not the official military.
A state in southern Sudan now under RSF control.
The government-like administration the RSF declared in areas it controls.

stories.headline: Aid cuts force UN food agency to stop feeding half a million people in Gaza each month
stories.dek: WFP now helps 1.1 million people, down from 1.6 million this summer. It needs more than £300 million to restore aid.
stories.caveman: More than a year after a ceasefire, Gaza still hasn't been rebuilt, there are few jobs, and most people depend on aid to eat. The UN's World Food Programme (WFP) fed about 1.6 million people there this summer. But its funding has fallen by more than half compared with 2025. So from October it cut help to 1.1 million people a month — meaning more than half a million lost support. Ration boxes, cash for food and hot meals were all cut back. WFP needs more than £300 million over six months. A UNICEF survey found 1 in 8 children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter is coming, and hunger in Gaza could get worse again. The famine declared in 2025 ended because of big aid deliveries; WFP says those gains are fragile.
stories.camps: Aid groups: donors, especially after the Trump administration gutted USAID, have pulled back and families are paying the price; reconstruction and jobs are needed so people don't rely on handouts forever. Donor side: many donor governments have cut aid budgets overall, and promised reconstruction under the ceasefire has not started, so there is no quick fix; WFP says rebuilding the economy is the only way to end dependence on handouts.
stories.image_alt: WFP workers serve hot meals at a community kitchen in Gaza
stories.image_credit: Photo: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFP via The Guardian

terms.explain: The UN agency that gives food aid in emergencies.
When a child is too short for their age because of long-term poor nutrition; it can cause lasting harm.
An agreement to stop fighting.
The US government agency that gave aid abroad; it was largely dismantled by the Trump administration.
A global scale for measuring hunger; phase 5 is famine.

stories.headline: HelloFresh warehouse temp workers say they were abused, threatened with ICE and denied bathroom breaks
stories.dek: An amended class-action complaint over the Newark, New Jersey facility goes before a judge on Oct. 23. HelloFresh denies everything.
stories.caveman: HelloFresh sends meal kits to people's homes. Temp workers at its Newark, New Jersey facility, most of them Hispanic, filed a class-action lawsuit in 2024. A newly proposed amended complaint says managers took ID badges workers needed to leave, threatened to call immigration agents (ICE), physically and verbally abused them, sexually harassed Hispanic women, limited bathroom breaks, and scolded them for speaking Spanish. One ex-worker told the Guardian the bathroom limits caused him incontinence problems. A New Jersey judge will look at the amended complaint on Oct. 23.
stories.why_it_matters: Many warehouse jobs are filled through temp agencies, often by immigrants who may fear speaking up. The case shows how hard it is to hold big brands responsible for subcontracted workers.
stories.camps: Workers: say they were given the hardest jobs and treated worse because they are Latino, and were afraid to complain. HelloFresh: denies all the claims, says an internal investigation found them "entirely without merit". The three staffing agencies did not comment but have asked the court to dismiss the case.
stories.image_alt: Contents of a HelloFresh meal kit (2018 file photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Kristoffer Tripplaar/Alamy via The Guardian

terms.explain: A lawsuit where one or a few people sue on behalf of a whole group with the same complaint.
Someone hired through a staffing agency to work at another company, often short-term.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that arrests and deports immigrants.
A company that supplies workers to other businesses.
An updated version of the claims in a lawsuit, adding new details.
